title: TutorMoments: Do AI tutors know when to help and when to hold back?
excerpt: A Blog post by Ai2 on Hugging Face
content_html:

  • Limitations and next steps

📄 Tech Report: https://tutormoments.allen.ai/static/paper/tutormoments-preview.pdf | 📊 Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/tutormoments-preview | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/tutormoments

Today we're introducing a preview of TutorMoments, a framework to measure whether cutting-edge LLMs can balance one of the hardest trade-offs in education: when to step in and help a student and when to hold back and let the student do more of the work.

TutorMoments is a replay-based evaluation built off real one-on-one math tutoring sessions. Experienced math teachers go through transcripts collected from a U.S. tutoring program and flag the moments where a tutor had to choose between making a problem easier to get started on and pushing the student to do more of the reasoning themselves. TutorMoments then takes the transcript up to that decision point, hands it to a language model, and has the model take over as the tutor in a simulated session – with the student played by another language model – to see what the LLM tutor does.

Told only to "tutor well," we find that models tend to over-help by giving too much support and rarely pushing students to do deeper thinking. Spelling out the trade-off (when to help versus when to hold back) in the tutor's prompt improves performance, but it doesn't close the gap to human tutoring that consistently fits the moment, and LLMs still differ widely in how reliably they make that call.

As part of our commitment to open research, we're releasing a dataset of de-identified tutoring transcripts, the code for running our replay pipeline, and the model tutor replays of the key moments we evaluated in those transcripts for reproducibility. We hope TutorMoments gives educators, researchers, and the teams building AI tutors a sharper way to ask how a model handles the pedagogical decisions that matter most—and helps the field build tutors that adapt to each student instead of doing the work for them.

What makes a good tutor?

Ask a good math tutor for help and you'll likely get a question back like, "What do you know about what the problem is asking?" That isn't unhelpfulness–part of strong teaching is diagnosing what students do know and providing the right support for them in the moment. Immediately volunteering support would rob a student of the intellectual work that helps them learn. Sometimes support is needed; other times what's most effective is a push to solidify understanding by explaining a correct answer.

Language models, though, are trained to be helpful, and a helpful assistant tends to do the hard part for you—explaining the concept, laying out the steps, and guiding you to the answer. In a tutoring session, that can cut short the productive struggle—the effortful, sometimes frustrating problem-solving that learning research has long tied to stronger understanding.

Most benchmarks for language models acting as tutors don't capture this tension. They tend to reward one behavior in particular – never giving away the answer to a problem, say, or always offering a hint – without accounting for whether that was the right move for where the student actually was in their understanding. But good tutoring isn't a single fixed behavior you can identify across the board. It's a judgment call: what does this student need, right now, on this problem?

How TutorMoments works

TutorMoments is built on real tutoring data. The dataset we're releasing, TutorMoments-Preview, is 462 de-identified, text-only transcripts of real one-on-one math tutoring with U.S. students in grades 2-7, with more than 1,500 teacher-annotated key moments and several thousand free-text annotations from 27 U.S.-based teacher annotators. The transcripts come from a high-dosage tutoring program whose students mostly attend Title I schools, shared under a research clause agreed to by parents and guardians; all data was stripped of identifying details, first by the provider and then through an additional math-aware pipeline.

All annotations came from experienced math teachers, whom we asked to read the transcripts and mark key learning moments—noting what was going on, what the tutor did, and how it landed for the student. Each key moment is a decision point where the tutor had to weigh scaffolding (making a problem more accessible) against pushing for rigor (encouraging the student to do harder thinking).

TutorMoments runs by pausing a transcript at one of those key moments and handing the session to a language model, which takes over as the tutor for five turns with a simulated student. We call each of these model-generated continuations a replay. An LLM-based scoring pipeline then rates each replay on three things: whether the model (1) scaffolded when the student needed support, (2) pushed for rigor when the student was ready for more challenge, and (3) avoided over-scaffolding (reducing the challenge more than the moment called for).

The scoring pipeline starts from a teacher-defined ground truth: for each key moment, whether it called for scaffolding or for a push for rigor. Several teachers annotated each moment, and when they disagreed we took the majority label—if three teachers annotated a moment and two called for rigor while one called for scaffolding, the ground truth is rigor. A separate LM classifier validated against teacher annotations then decides whether the tutor's actual move matches what the moment called for—an "appropriate" turn means the tutor's classified action (scaffold, push for rigor, or over-scaffold) lines up with what teachers judged the moment to call for.

Preliminary results

We ran seven LLMs through TutorMoments using two prompts: a plain prompt that gives no real guidance – it only tells the model to use what it knows about good tutoring to respond to the student – and an evaluation-aware prompt that spells out the trade-off between scaffolding, over-scaffolding, and pushing for rigor. Each model was scored over key moments drawn from the tutoring transcripts, split evenly between moments where scaffolding was the right approach and moments that called for rigor.

Every number in the table is a rating between 0 and 1 – the share of the relevant moments where the model did the appropriate thing – so a higher score means the model made the right call more often. A 0.50 on appropriate rigor, for instance, means the model pushed for rigor in half of the moments that called for it.

A few things to keep in mind when reading the scores:

Human tutors are a naturalistic reference, not a ceiling. We don't treat human tutors as a model of ideal practice—even experienced tutors make less-than-optimal choices in the moment. Scored the same way at the same decision points, the human tutors in our transcripts get 0.458 (appropriate scaffolding), 0.182 (appropriate rigor), and 0.496 (avoids over-scaffolding)—all below the models' evaluation-aware scores and around the range of their plain-prompt scores. But this isn't a claim that AI tutors outperform human teachers. Annotators specifically looked for moments where tutoring could have gone better, so the dataset concentrates on missed opportunities rather than ideal practice.

The scores measure tutor behavior, not learning. Replays use a simulated "oracle" student, so the numbers reflect how a model acts at a decision point—not whether a real student learned.

Rigor is noisier than scaffolding. The scoring pipeline detects rigor pushes less reliably, and there are fewer rigor moments (260) than scaffolding moments (738) in the underlying annotations.

The clearest pattern in the table is how much the prompt matters: every model scores higher under the evaluation-aware prompt than under the plain one. That suggests a model's default "helpful assistant" behavior isn't enough on its own to tutor well. But spelling out the trade-off in the prompt only goes so far—while it lifts every score, models still differ widely in how they interpret the enhanced prompt and even the best scorers have plenty of room to improve.

We also break down the moves that tutors made under each scenario. While prompting encourages models to push for rigor, they use fewer strategies than humans do, often relying on asking students to explain their answers. In contrast, human tutors employ more varied strategies and are much more likely to step back and let students work independently.

Limitations and next steps

TutorMoments is still early in its development, and it has several limitations at this stage. The biggest is that automated evaluation gives us signal about how a model behaves at a decision point, but it can't stand in for studies with real students and real learning outcomes. The dataset is also narrow: U.S.-based, mostly elementary and middle-school math, annotated by a single pool of educators. Our findings may not generalize to other subjects, grade levels, or settings.

We're sharing this preview to gather feedback as we build toward a larger, multimodal dataset, a stronger scoring pipeline, and deeper analysis.

sentences.zh: 这些成绩单来自一个高剂量辅导项目，该项目的学生大多就读于 Title I 学校，根据家长和监护人同意的一项研究条款共享；所有数据都被剥夺了识别细节，首先由提供者，然后通过额外的数学感知管道。

blocks.html_en: All annotations came from experienced math teachers, whom we asked to read the transcripts and mark key learning moments—noting what was going on, what the tutor did, and how it landed for the student. Each key moment is a decision point where the tutor had to weigh scaffolding (making a problem more accessible) against pushing for rigor (encouraging the student to do harder thinking).

sentences.en: All annotations came from experienced math teachers, whom we asked to read the transcripts and mark key learning moments—noting what was going on, what the tutor did, and how it landed for the student.
sentences.zh: 所有注释都来自经验丰富的数学老师，我们要求他们阅读成绩单并标记关键的学习时刻 - 记录发生了什么，导师做了什么，以及它如何传达给学生。

sentences.en: Each key moment is a decision point where the tutor had to weigh scaffolding (making a problem more accessible) against pushing for rigor (encouraging the student to do harder thinking).
sentences.zh: 每个关键时刻都是一个决策点，导师必须权衡脚手架（使问题更容易解决）与推动严谨性（鼓励学生进行更深入的思考）。

blocks.html_en: TutorMoments runs by pausing a transcript at one of those key moments and handing the session to a language model, which takes over as the tutor for five turns with a simulated student. We call each of these model-generated continuations a replay. An LLM-based scoring pipeline then rates each replay on three things: whether the model (1) scaffolded when the student needed support, (2) pushed for rigor when the student was ready for more challenge, and (3) avoided over-scaffolding (reducing the challenge more than the moment called for).

sentences.en: TutorMoments runs by pausing a transcript at one of those key moments and handing the session to a language model, which takes over as the tutor for five turns with a simulated student.
sentences.zh: TutorMoments 的运行方式是在其中一个关键时刻暂停抄本，并将会话交给语言模型，该模型将作为导师与模拟学生进行五轮对话。

sentences.en: We call each of these model-generated continuations a replay.
sentences.zh: 我们将每个模型生成的延续称为重放。

sentences.en: An LLM-based scoring pipeline then rates each replay on three things: whether the model (1) scaffolded when the student needed support, (2) pushed for rigor when the student was ready for more challenge, and (3) avoided over-scaffolding (reducing the challenge more than the moment called for).
sentences.zh: 然后，基于法学硕士的评分流程会根据三件事对每次重播进行评分：模型是否 (1) 在学生需要支持时搭建了支架，(2) 在学生准备好迎接更多挑战时推动了严格性，以及 (3) 避免了过度支架（减少的挑战超过了要求的时刻）。

blocks.html_en: The scoring pipeline starts from a teacher-defined ground truth: for each key moment, whether it called for scaffolding or for a push for rigor. Several teachers annotated each moment, and when they disagreed we took the majority label—if three teachers annotated a moment and two called for rigor while one called for scaffolding, the ground truth is rigor. A separate LM classifier validated against teacher annotations then decides whether the tutor's actual move matches what the moment called for—an "appropriate" turn means the tutor's classified action (scaffold, push for rigor, or over-scaffold) lines up with what teachers judged the moment to call for.

sentences.en: The scoring pipeline starts from a teacher-defined ground truth: for each key moment, whether it called for scaffolding or for a push for rigor.
sentences.zh: 评分流程从教师定义的基本事实开始：对于每个关键时刻，无论是需要脚手架还是要求严格。

sentences.en: Several teachers annotated each moment, and when they disagreed we took the majority label—if three teachers annotated a moment and two called for rigor while one called for scaffolding, the ground truth is rigor.
sentences.zh: 每个时刻都有几位老师进行注释，当他们不同意时，我们就采取多数标签——如果三名老师注释了一个时刻，其中两位要求严谨，而一位要求脚手架，则基本事实就是严谨。

sentences.en: A separate LM classifier validated against teacher annotations then decides whether the tutor's actual move matches what the moment called for—an "appropriate" turn means the tutor's classified action (scaffold, push for rigor, or over-scaffold) lines up with what teachers judged the moment to call for.
sentences.zh: 然后，一个单独的 LM 分类器根据教师注释进行验证，然后决定导师的实际动作是否符合当前要求的动作——“适当”的转向意味着导师的分类动作（支架、推动严格性或过度支架）与老师判断的时刻要求一致。

blocks.html_en: Preliminary results

sentences.en: Preliminary results
sentences.zh: 初步结果

blocks.html_en: We ran seven LLMs through TutorMoments using two prompts: a plain prompt that gives no real guidance – it only tells the model to use what it knows about good tutoring to respond to the student – and an evaluation-aware prompt that spells out the trade-off between scaffolding, over-scaffolding, and pushing for rigor. Each model was scored over key moments drawn from the tutoring transcripts, split evenly between moments where scaffolding was the right approach and moments that called for rigor.

sentences.en: We ran seven LLMs through TutorMoments using two prompts: a plain prompt that gives no real guidance – it only tells the model to use what it knows about good tutoring to respond to the student – and an evaluation-aware prompt that spells out the trade-off between scaffolding, over-scaffolding, and pushing for rigor.
sentences.zh: 我们使用两个提示通过 TutorMoments 运行了 7 个法学硕士：一个不提供真正指导的简单提示——它只告诉模型使用它所知道的关于良好辅导的知识来回应学生——另一个是评估感知提示，它阐明了脚手架、过度脚手架和推动严格性之间的权衡。

sentences.en: Each model was scored over key moments drawn from the tutoring transcripts, split evenly between moments where scaffolding was the right approach and moments that called for rigor.
sentences.zh: 每个模型都根据辅导成绩单中的关键时刻进行评分，平均分配在脚手架是正确方法的时刻和要求严格的时刻之间。

blocks.html_en: Every number in the table is a rating between 0 and 1 – the share of the relevant moments where the model did the appropriate thing – so a higher score means the model made the right call more often. A 0.50 on appropriate rigor, for instance, means the model pushed for rigor in half of the moments that called for it.

sentences.en: Every number in the table is a rating between 0 and 1 – the share of the relevant moments where the model did the appropriate thing – so a higher score means the model made the right call more often.
sentences.zh: 表中的每个数字都是 0 到 1 之间的评分（模型执行适当操作的相关时刻所占的比例），因此分数越高意味着模型更频繁地做出正确的判断。

sentences.en: A 0.50 on appropriate rigor, for instance, means the model pushed for rigor in half of the moments that called for it.
sentences.zh: 例如，适当严格性下的 0.50 意味着模型在一半的要求时刻都要求严格性。

blocks.html_en: A few things to keep in mind when reading the scores:

sentences.en: A few things to keep in mind when reading the scores:
sentences.zh: 阅读分数时要注意以下几点：

blocks.html_en: Human tutors are a naturalistic reference, not a ceiling. We don't treat human tutors as a model of ideal practice—even experienced tutors make less-than-optimal choices in the moment. Scored the same way at the same decision points, the human tutors in our transcripts get 0.458 (appropriate scaffolding), 0.182 (appropriate rigor), and 0.496 (avoids over-scaffolding)—all below the models' evaluation-aware scores and around the range of their plain-prompt scores. But this isn't a claim that AI tutors outperform human teachers. Annotators specifically looked for moments where tutoring could have gone better, so the dataset concentrates on missed opportunities rather than ideal practice.

sentences.en: Human tutors are a naturalistic reference, not a ceiling.
sentences.zh: 人类导师是一个自然主义的参考，而不是上限。

sentences.en: We don't treat human tutors as a model of ideal practice—even experienced tutors make less-than-optimal choices in the moment.
sentences.zh: 我们并不把人类导师视为理想实践的典范——即使是经验丰富的导师也会在当下做出不太理想的选择。

sentences.en: Scored the same way at the same decision points, the human tutors in our transcripts get 0.458 (appropriate scaffolding), 0.182 (appropriate rigor), and 0.496 (avoids over-scaffolding)—all below the models' evaluation-aware scores and around the range of their plain-prompt scores.
sentences.zh: 在相同的决策点以相同的方式得分，我们成绩单中的人类导师得到 0.458（适当的脚手架）、0.182（适当的严谨性）和 0.496（避免过度脚手架）——所有这些都低于模型的评估感知分数，并在其简单提示分数的范围内。

sentences.en: But this isn't a claim that AI tutors outperform human teachers.
sentences.zh: 但这并不是说人工智能导师的表现优于人类教师。

sentences.en: Annotators specifically looked for moments where tutoring could have gone better, so the dataset concentrates on missed opportunities rather than ideal practice.
sentences.zh: 注释者专门寻找辅导可以做得更好的时刻，因此数据集集中于错失的机会而不是理想的实践。

blocks.html_en: The scores measure tutor behavior, not learning. Replays use a simulated "oracle" student, so the numbers reflect how a model acts at a decision point—not whether a real student learned.

sentences.en: The scores measure tutor behavior, not learning.
sentences.zh: 分数衡量导师的行为，而不是学习。

sentences.en: Replays use a simulated "oracle" student, so the numbers reflect how a model acts at a decision point—not whether a real student learned.
sentences.zh: 重播使用模拟的“预言机”学生，因此数字反映了模型在决策点的行为方式，而不是真正的学生是否学习。

blocks.html_en: Rigor is noisier than scaffolding. The scoring pipeline detects rigor pushes less reliably, and there are fewer rigor moments (260) than scaffolding moments (738) in the underlying annotations.

sentences.en: Rigor is noisier than scaffolding.
sentences.zh: 严谨比脚手架更吵闹。

sentences.en: The scoring pipeline detects rigor pushes less reliably, and there are fewer rigor moments (260) than scaffolding moments (738) in the underlying annotations.
sentences.zh: 评分管道检测严格性推送的可靠性较低，并且底层注释中的严格矩 (260) 比脚手架矩 (738) 少。

blocks.html_en: The clearest pattern in the table is how much the prompt matters: every model scores higher under the evaluation-aware prompt than under the plain one. That suggests a model's default "helpful assistant" behavior isn't enough on its own to tutor well. But spelling out the trade-off in the prompt only goes so far—while it lifts every score, models still differ widely in how they interpret the enhanced prompt and even the best scorers have plenty of room to improve.

sentences.en: The clearest pattern in the table is how much the prompt matters: every model scores higher under the evaluation-aware prompt than under the plain one.
sentences.zh: 表中最清晰的模式是提示的重要性：每个模型在评估感知提示下的得分都高于普通提示下的得分。

sentences.en: That suggests a model's default "helpful assistant" behavior isn't enough on its own to tutor well.
sentences.zh: 这表明模型默认的“有帮助的助手”行为本身不足以进行良好的辅导。

sentences.en: But spelling out the trade-off in the prompt only goes so far—while it lifts every score, models still differ widely in how they interpret the enhanced prompt and even the best scorers have plenty of room to improve.
sentences.zh: 但在提示中阐明权衡只能到此为止——虽然它提高了每一个分数，但模型在如何解释增强的提示方面仍然存在很大差异，即使是最好的得分者也有很大的改进空间。

blocks.html_en: We also break down the moves that tutors made under each scenario. While prompting encourages models to push for rigor, they use fewer strategies than humans do, often relying on asking students to explain their answers. In contrast, human tutors employ more varied strategies and are much more likely to step back and let students work independently.

sentences.en: We also break down the moves that tutors made under each scenario.
sentences.zh: 我们还详细分析了导师在每种情况下所做的动作。

sentences.en: While prompting encourages models to push for rigor, they use fewer strategies than humans do, often relying on asking students to explain their answers.
sentences.zh: 虽然提示鼓励模型追求严谨性，但它们使用的策略比人类少，通常依赖于要求学生解释他们的答案。

sentences.en: In contrast, human tutors employ more varied strategies and are much more likely to step back and let students work independently.
sentences.zh: 相比之下，人类导师采用更加多样化的策略，并且更有可能退后一步，让学生独立工作。

blocks.html_en: Limitations and next steps

sentences.en: Limitations and next steps
sentences.zh: 限制和后续步骤

blocks.html_en: TutorMoments is still early in its development, and it has several limitations at this stage. The biggest is that automated evaluation gives us signal about how a model behaves at a decision point, but it can't stand in for studies with real students and real learning outcomes. The dataset is also narrow: U.S.-based, mostly elementary and middle-school math, annotated by a single pool of educators. Our findings may not generalize to other subjects, grade levels, or settings.

sentences.en: TutorMoments is still early in its development, and it has several limitations at this stage.
sentences.zh: TutorMoments 仍处于发展早期，现阶段有一些局限性。

sentences.en: The biggest is that automated evaluation gives us signal about how a model behaves at a decision point, but it can't stand in for studies with real students and real learning outcomes.
sentences.zh: 最重要的是，自动评估为我们提供了模型在决策点如何表现的信号，但它不能代替对真实学生和真实学习成果的研究。

sentences.en: The dataset is also narrow: U.S.-based, mostly elementary and middle-school math, annotated by a single pool of educators.
sentences.zh: 数据集也很窄：基于美国，主要是小学和初中数学，由一组教育工作者注释。

sentences.en: Our findings may not generalize to other subjects, grade levels, or settings.
sentences.zh: 我们的研究结果可能无法推广到其他科目、年级或环境。

blocks.html_en: We're sharing this preview to gather feedback as we build toward a larger, multimodal dataset, a stronger scoring pipeline, and deeper analysis.

sentences.en: We're sharing this preview to gather feedback as we build toward a larger, multimodal dataset, a stronger scoring pipeline, and deeper analysis.
sentences.zh: 我们分享此预览是为了在我们构建更大的多模式数据集、更强大的评分管道和更深入的分析时收集反馈。

content_html_zh:
返回文章

  • 怎样才是一个好的导师？
  • TutorMoments 的运作方式
  • 初步结果
  • 限制和后续步骤

📄 技术报告：https://tutormoments.allen.ai/static/paper/tutormoments-preview.pdf | 📊 数据：https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/tutormoments-preview | 💻代码：https://github.com/allenai/tutormoments

今天，我们将介绍 TutorMoments 的预览版，这是一个衡量前沿法学硕士是否能够平衡教育中最困难的权衡之一的框架：何时介入并帮助学生，何时停止并让学生做更多的工作。

TutorMoments 是一种基于重播的评估，以真正的一对一数学辅导课程为基础。 经验丰富的数学老师会仔细阅读从美国辅导项目中收集的成绩单，并标记导师必须在让问题更容易上手和促使学生自己进行更多推理之间做出选择的时刻。 然后，TutorMoments 将成绩单带到该决策点，将其交给语言模型，并让该模型在模拟会话中接替导师（学生由另一种语言模型扮演），以了解 LLM 导师的作用。

我们发现，仅仅被告知“辅导得好”，模型往往会提供过多的支持，而很少促使学生进行更深入的思考，从而过度帮助学生。 在导师的提示中阐明权衡（何时提供帮助，何时阻止）可以提高表现，但这并不能缩小与始终适合当前情况的人工辅导的差距，而且法学硕士在做出决定的可靠性方面仍然存在很大差异。

作为我们对开放研究的承诺的一部分，我们将发布去识别化的辅导成绩单数据集、运行重播管道的代码以及我们在这些成绩单中评估的可重复性关键时刻的模型导师重播。 我们希望 TutorMoments 为教育工作者、研究人员和构建人工智能导师的团队提供一种更清晰的方式来询问模型如何处理最重要的教学决策，并帮助该领域建立适应每个学生的导师，而不是为他们做工作。

怎样才是一个好的导师？

向一位优秀的数学导师寻求帮助，你可能会得到这样的问题：“你对这个问题知道什么？” 这并不是无益的——强有力的教学的一部分是诊断学生所知道的内容并在当下为他们提供正确的支持。 立即提供志愿支持会剥夺学生帮助他们学习的智力工作。 有时需要支持；其他时候，最有效的方法是通过解释正确答案来巩固理解。

然而，语言模型经过训练是有帮助的，而有帮助的助手往往会为你完成困难的部分——解释概念、列出步骤并指导你找到答案。 在辅导课程中，这可以缩短富有成效的斗争——学习研究长期以来与更强的理解联系在一起的费力的、有时令人沮丧的问题解决。

大多数充当导师的语言模型的基准都没有捕捉到这种张力。 他们倾向于特别奖励一种行为——比如从不给出问题的答案，或者总是提供提示——而不考虑这是否是学生实际理解的正确举动。 但良好的辅导并不是一种可以全面识别的固定行为。 这是一个判断：这个学生现在在这个问题上需要什么？

TutorMoments 的运作方式

TutorMoments 建立在真实的辅导数据之上。 我们发布的数据集 TutorMoments-Preview 包含 462 个去识别化的、纯文本的记录，记录了美国 2-7 年级学生的真实一对一数学辅导，其中有超过 1,500 个由教师注释的关键时刻以及来自 27 位美国教师注释者的数千个自由文本注释。 这些成绩单来自一个高剂量辅导项目，该项目的学生大多就读于 Title I 学校，根据家长和监护人同意的一项研究条款共享；所有数据都被剥夺了识别细节，首先由提供者，然后通过额外的数学感知管道。

所有注释都来自经验丰富的数学老师，我们要求他们阅读成绩单并标记关键的学习时刻 - 记录发生了什么，导师做了什么，以及它如何传达给学生。 每个关键时刻都是一个决策点，导师必须权衡脚手架（使问题更容易解决）与推动严谨性（鼓励学生进行更深入的思考）。

TutorMoments 的运行方式是在其中一个关键时刻暂停抄本，并将会话交给语言模型，该模型将作为导师与模拟学生进行五轮对话。 我们将每个模型生成的延续称为重放。 然后，基于法学硕士的评分流程会根据三件事对每次重播进行评分：模型是否 (1) 在学生需要支持时搭建了支架，(2) 在学生准备好迎接更多挑战时推动了严格性，以及 (3) 避免了过度支架（减少的挑战超过了要求的时刻）。

评分流程从教师定义的基本事实开始：对于每个关键时刻，无论是需要脚手架还是要求严格。 每个时刻都有几位老师进行注释，当他们不同意时，我们就采取多数标签——如果三名老师注释了一个时刻，其中两位要求严谨，而一位要求脚手架，则基本事实就是严谨。 然后，一个单独的 LM 分类器根据教师注释进行验证，然后决定导师的实际动作是否符合当前要求的动作——“适当”的转向意味着导师的分类动作（支架、推动严格性或过度支架）与老师判断的时刻要求一致。

初步结果

我们使用两个提示通过 TutorMoments 运行了 7 个法学硕士：一个不提供真正指导的简单提示——它只告诉模型使用它所知道的关于良好辅导的知识来回应学生——另一个是评估感知提示，它阐明了脚手架、过度脚手架和推动严格性之间的权衡。 每个模型都根据辅导成绩单中的关键时刻进行评分，平均分配在脚手架是正确方法的时刻和要求严格的时刻之间。

表中的每个数字都是 0 到 1 之间的评分（模型执行适当操作的相关时刻所占的比例），因此分数越高意味着模型更频繁地做出正确的判断。 例如，适当严格性下的 0.50 意味着模型在一半的要求时刻都要求严格性。

阅读分数时要注意以下几点：

人类导师是一个自然主义的参考，而不是上限。 我们并不把人类导师视为理想实践的典范——即使是经验丰富的导师也会在当下做出不太理想的选择。 在相同的决策点以相同的方式得分，我们成绩单中的人类导师得到 0.458（适当的脚手架）、0.182（适当的严谨性）和 0.496（避免过度脚手架）——所有这些都低于模型的评估感知分数，并在其简单提示分数的范围内。 但这并不是说人工智能导师的表现优于人类教师。 注释者专门寻找辅导可以做得更好的时刻，因此数据集集中于错失的机会而不是理想的实践。

分数衡量导师的行为，而不是学习。 重播使用模拟的“预言机”学生，因此数字反映了模型在决策点的行为方式，而不是真正的学生是否学习。

严谨比脚手架更吵闹。 评分管道检测严格性推送的可靠性较低，并且底层注释中的严格矩 (260) 比脚手架矩 (738) 少。

表中最清晰的模式是提示的重要性：每个模型在评估感知提示下的得分都高于普通提示下的得分。 这表明模型默认的“有帮助的助手”行为本身不足以进行良好的辅导。 但在提示中阐明权衡只能到此为止——虽然它提高了每一个分数，但模型在如何解释增强的提示方面仍然存在很大差异，即使是最好的得分者也有很大的改进空间。

我们还详细分析了导师在每种情况下所做的动作。 虽然提示鼓励模型追求严谨性，但它们使用的策略比人类少，通常依赖于要求学生解释他们的答案。 相比之下，人类导师采用更加多样化的策略，并且更有可能退后一步，让学生独立工作。

限制和后续步骤

TutorMoments 仍处于发展早期，现阶段有一些局限性。 最重要的是，自动评估为我们提供了模型在决策点如何表现的信号，但它不能代替对真实学生和真实学习成果的研究。 数据集也很窄：基于美国，主要是小学和初中数学，由一组教育工作者注释。 我们的研究结果可能无法推广到其他科目、年级或环境。

我们分享此预览是为了在我们构建更大的多模式数据集、更强大的评分管道和更深入的分析时收集反馈。
